title: Preemptive Multitasking in 64 Kilobytes
content:
The claim sounds impossible and it is not, but only just. What has actually been built is a preemptive multitasking graphical operating system for Z80 machines, running on hardware from 1984, managing up to a megabyte of banked memory, with a microkernel and a windowed environment. It is called SymbOS, and looking at how it is put together is the most useful thing I have read about kernel design in some time.
Three services and nothing else. The kernel handles task management, memory management, and inter-process communication. That is the whole microkernel. Everything else, including networking, sound and printing, is a daemon that lives outside the core and is loaded when something needs it.
The result is that the kernel fits in an unexpanded 128 KB machine, which matters because the alternative was that a system requiring 128 KB of RAM was a system half the machines in the target market could not run.
Memory, in 256-byte blocks. Dynamic allocation happens in 256-byte chunks, up to 1024 KB, reached by bank switching past the Z80’s 64 KB address space. There is no memory protection, which is a deliberate choice and worth respecting: on hardware this constrained, protection is expensive and the benefit is small, since the failure mode it prevents is a program crashing itself.
IPC through messages, not calls. Processes talk by passing messages, both synchronous and asynchronous, rather than by calling into each other. This is the single most consequential decision in the design and it is what makes the rest tractable: with message passing, a process does not need to know where another process lives, which matters enormously when the whole address space can move under you.
Why a Z80 could do this at all. The processor has properties that made a modern-style kernel possible, and they are not obvious until you look. The stack pointer is freely relocatable, which the 6502’s is not, and the alternate register set can be swapped with a single four-T-state instruction, which is fast enough to make context switching cheap.
SymbOS mixes preemptive and cooperative multitasking: some tasks are interrupted after a time quantum, others yield voluntarily, and priority levels decide which runs when. The hybrid lets a foreground task stay responsive without making everything else a priority-zero busy loop.
The current release supports the Amstrad CPC, MSX2 and later, the Amstrad PCW, the Enterprise, and the ZX Spectrum Next. Boot requires 128 KB of RAM unexpanded.
The other three FreeDOS is the one that turned out to matter commercially. It started as a manifesto in 1994 proposing a public-domain DOS after Microsoft announced it was ending sales, and the kernel is an independent from-scratch implementation of the MS-DOS API written in C and assembly, released under the GPL. It has never been derived from Microsoft’s source, which is the detail that matters: it is a reimplementation from documentation, like AROS, and like AROS it runs software that was never meant to run on it.
It is still shipping. There is a kernel release track that continues, test distributions every month, and it is used inside Dell, HP and Intel for BIOS and firmware update paths. A thirty-year-old clean-room DOS is somebody’s supported dependency.
KolibriOS is the aesthetic opposite: an x86 system written almost entirely in FASM assembly, which boots in seconds and fits on a 1.44 MB floppy including a GUI, a web browser and multitasking. The assembly is the point, not nostalgia. It is a direct route to small, fast, and a claim you can verify by looking at the image size.
AROS takes the same approach as FreeDOS from the other direction: a reimplementation of the AmigaOS API, the way Wine is to Windows, rather than a machine emulator. Its own documentation is honest about the trade, and the trade is that AROS wants native applications and is faster for them, while an emulator wants binary compatibility including code that pokes hardware, and runs more software as a result.
There is now a middle path worth watching: a transparent m68k compatibility layer for AROS on x86 and ARM, which runs existing Amiga binaries by emulating the CPU and routing API calls to native implementations. Eight hundred and ten auto-generated thunks across seventeen libraries. That is Wine’s trick, applied to an operating system most people assume is gone.
Why this is worth reading A microkernel that fits in the memory of a 1984 machine, doing three jobs, and communicating by message passing, is a better description of what a microservice is than most things written about microservices. The constraints did not make the design worse. They made it legible.
